passage:
Nisha: Are you coming Saturday? Everyone's asking.
Hansa: I don't think so. Arohi gets upset when I go out without her.
Nisha: You've cancelled the last four things.
Hansa: I know. She says my friends don't really care about me and she's the only one who does. Some days I almost believe it.
Nisha: Han, we do care. I miss you.
Hansa: I miss you too. I've even stopped calling my mother as much because Arohi says it's clingy.
Nisha: That doesn't sound like you. Can I call you tomorrow, just us?
Hansa: Yes. Please.
Nisha: I'm here. Whenever you want.

qa.q: How many recent things has Hansa cancelled, according to Nisha?
qa.a: Nisha says Hansa has cancelled the last four things.

qa.q: What is Hansa feeling when writing that some days she almost believes Arohi?
qa.a: Hansa feels lonely and unsure, and has started to half-believe that only Arohi cares. Missing Nisha and her mother shows the pull the other way.

qa.q: What could Hansa do to keep an outside connection?
qa.a: She can accept Nisha's call, keep in touch with her mother and friends, and reach out to someone she trusts if the distance keeps growing.

qa.q: How does Nisha see Hansa's recent changes?
qa.a: Nisha notices the cancelled plans and says the change does not sound like Hansa. She misses her and offers a private call without judging.

grounding: A partner gradually distances the protagonist from friends and family; she keeps one outside connection by confiding in Nisha.

passage:
'You're going to the Sunday match again?' Suraj asked from the sofa.
'It's just the old college gang. Once a week.'
'Those guys don't even like me. And your Amma calls every day. When do we get time?'
'We live together, Suraj. We get every evening.'
'Fine. Go. I'll just sit here.'
Jatin stopped at the door. 'Last month it was my cousin's birthday. Before that, Amma's lunch. I've skipped a lot of things.'
'Because you wanted to be with me.'
'Because you sulked every time.' Jatin picked up his kit. 'I'm going. And I'm going to tell Farid what's been happening. I need at least one person outside this flat to talk to.'
'You'll make me the villain.'
'I'll just say what happened.'
Walking to the ground, Jatin rang Farid first.

qa.q: What event is Jatin going to on Sunday?
qa.a: Jatin is going to the Sunday match with the old college gang.

qa.q: What might Jatin be feeling as he stops at the door?
qa.a: Jatin feels uneasy and sad, realising how many family events have been skipped because of Suraj's sulking.
Going to the match and ringing Farid, because it keeps an outside connection who can help Jatin see the pattern.

qa.q: How does Suraj see Jatin's friends and family?
qa.a: Suraj treats them as rivals for Jatin's time and fears that talking to Farid will make Suraj look like the villain.

grounding: Shows a partner slowly pulling Jatin away from family and friends, and Jatin keeping an outside connection and reaching out to someone he trusts.

passage: My name's Siddharth, and it took me most of second year to see it. Tarun never said, 'Don't meet your friends.' He said things like, 'Imtiaz's jokes are a bit cruel, no?' or 'Your hostel group chat is so childish.' So I muted the chat. I skipped the Holi party because Tarun looked hurt. I stopped calling home on Sundays because we were always 'doing something'. By March I was eating in the mess alone most nights. What woke me up was my roommate Imtiaz leaving a sticky note on my laptop: 'Miss you, yaar. Chai at 9?' I went. I cried a little over the chai, which surprised us both, and I told him everything. I haven't worked it all out yet, but I call home again now, and Imtiaz is the one outside line I don't let go of.

qa.q: What did Imtiaz write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Imtiaz wrote, 'Miss you, yaar. Chai at 9?'

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling over the chai with Imtiaz?
qa.a: Siddharth felt lonely and relieved at once, crying a little after months of drifting away from friends.

qa.q: What would you advise someone noticing the same drift?
qa.a: Reach out to one trusted person, as Siddharth did with Imtiaz, and keep that connection even if a partner frowns on it.

qa.q: How might Tarun see the hostel friends and the group chat?
qa.a: Tarun seems to see them as competition and quietly runs them down, so Siddharth pulls away without ever being told to.

grounding: A first-person account of a partner's small remarks cutting Siddharth off from friends and home, and the recovery of reaching back to one trusted person.
